title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: However little Elinor generally trusted Lucy’s truthfulness, serious reflection made it impossible to doubt her in this case. No imaginable advantage could justify the foolishness of inventing a lie of this kind. Elinor could therefore no longer doubt—could not dare to doubt—that Lucy’s account was true. Every probability and every piece of evidence supported it; nothing contradicted it except her own wishes. Their opportunities to know each other at Mr. Pratt’s house provided an undeniable and alarming foundation for everything else. Edward’s visit near Plymouth, his sadness, his dissatisfaction with his prospects, his uncertain behaviour towards herself, the Miss Steeles’ surprisingly intimate knowledge of Norland and its family connections, the portrait, the letter, the ring: together these made up a body of evidence that overcame every fear of judging him unfairly. His ill-treatment of her became an established fact which no affection could explain away. For a little while, resentment at his behaviour and indignation at having been deceived left her able to feel only for herself. But other thoughts and considerations soon followed. Had Edward deliberately deceived her? Had he pretended to feel affection which he did not feel? Was his engagement to Lucy founded on love? No: whatever it might once have been, she could not believe that it was now. His love belonged entirely to herself. About that she could not be mistaken. Her mother, her sisters, Fanny—everyone had recognised his affection for her at Norland. It had not been an illusion created by her own vanity. He certainly loved her. How that conviction softened her heart! How powerfully it persuaded her to forgive! He had been wrong, very wrong, to remain at Norland after he first realised that her influence over him was becoming stronger than it should. That could not be defended. But if he had hurt her, how much more deeply had he hurt himself? If her situation deserved pity, his was beyond hope. His lack of judgement had made her unhappy for a time; it seemed to have deprived him of any chance of ever being anything else. She might eventually recover her peace of mind; but what could _he_ look forward to? Could he ever be reasonably happy with Lucy Steele? Even leaving his love for herself entirely aside, could a man of his honesty, his sensitivity, and his cultivated understanding be content with such a wife—uneducated, calculating, and selfish?

The infatuation of a nineteen-year-old would naturally have blinded him to everything except her beauty and good temper. But the four years since then—years which, if sensibly spent, do so much to develop the understanding—must have opened his eyes to the shortcomings of her education. The same years, spent by Lucy in less cultivated company and more frivolous occupations, had perhaps taken away the simplicity which might once have given her beauty an appealing character.

When Elinor had imagined him wanting to marry herself, the difficulties his mother might raise had seemed great enough. How much greater would they be now, when the woman he was engaged to unquestionably had humbler connections, and probably less money, than she had herself? With his heart so far removed from Lucy, these obstacles might indeed make little demand on his patience. But how miserable must someone be when the prospect of opposition and unkindness from his family could come as a relief!

As these thoughts passed painfully through her mind, one after another, she wept more for him than for herself. The knowledge that she had done nothing to deserve her present unhappiness sustained her; the belief that Edward had done nothing to lose her respect consoled her. Even now, while the heavy blow was still fresh, she believed she could control herself well enough to keep her mother and sisters from suspecting the truth. And she fulfilled her own expectations so completely that, when she joined them at dinner only two hours after all her dearest hopes had been destroyed, nobody looking at the sisters could have guessed their feelings. Elinor was secretly mourning the obstacles that must separate her for ever from the man she loved. Marianne was privately considering the perfections of a man whose heart she believed entirely her own, and whom she expected to see in every carriage that came near their house.

Having to hide from her mother and Marianne what had been confided to her, though it demanded constant effort, did not make Elinor’s distress worse. On the contrary, she was relieved to be spared telling them something that would cause them such pain. She was also spared hearing them condemn Edward, as their excessive affection for her would probably lead them to do; and that was more than she felt capable of bearing.

She knew that neither their advice nor their conversation could help her. Their tenderness and sorrow would increase her distress, while their example would do nothing to encourage her self-control, and neither would their praise. Alone, she was stronger. Her own good sense supported her so effectively that her resolution remained as steady, and her outward cheerfulness as consistent, as feelings so painful and so recent could possibly allow.

Painful as her first conversation with Lucy on the subject had been, she soon began earnestly wishing to renew it, and for several reasons. She wanted to hear many of the details of the engagement again. She wanted a clearer understanding of what Lucy really felt for Edward, and whether there was any sincerity in her declarations of tender affection. Above all, she wanted her willingness to return to the subject, and her calm manner in discussing it, to convince Lucy that she took only a friend’s interest in it. She greatly feared that her involuntary agitation during their morning conversation must have left at least some doubt about that. It seemed very likely that Lucy was inclined to be jealous of her. Edward had plainly always spoken of her with high praise: that was clear not just from Lucy’s own account, but from her willingness, after so short an acquaintance, to trust Elinor with a secret which she admitted, and which plainly was, so important. Even Sir John’s joking information must have carried some weight. Indeed, while Elinor felt so certain within herself that Edward truly loved her, she needed no other calculation of probabilities to understand why Lucy should be jealous. The confidence itself proved that she was. What other reason could there have been for revealing the affair, except to make Elinor aware of Lucy’s stronger claim on Edward, and teach her to avoid him in future? She found little difficulty in understanding this much of her rival’s purpose. She was firmly determined to treat Lucy as every principle of honour and honesty required, to struggle against her own love for Edward, and to see him as little as possible. But she could not deny herself the comfort of trying to persuade Lucy that her heart had suffered no wound. And since she could now hear nothing more painful on the subject than she had heard already, she did not doubt her ability to listen calmly to the details a second time.

An opportunity did not immediately present itself, though Lucy was just as willing as Elinor to take advantage of one. The weather was seldom fine enough for a walk together, which would have given them the easiest way of separating from the others. And although they met at least every other evening, either at the park or at the cottage, and usually at the park, nobody could suppose that they met for conversation. Such an idea would never have entered the heads of Sir John or Lady Middleton. They were consequently allowed very little time for general conversation, and none at all for private discussion. They met to eat, drink, and laugh together, to play cards, or consequences, or any other game that made enough noise.

One or two such gatherings had passed without giving Elinor a chance to speak privately with Lucy when Sir John called at the cottage one morning. He begged them, as an act of charity, to dine with Lady Middleton that day. He had to attend his club at Exeter, and otherwise she would be entirely alone, apart from her mother and the two Miss Steeles. Elinor foresaw a better opportunity for her purpose in a gathering of this kind. Under Lady Middleton’s quiet, well-bred direction, they would have more freedom among themselves than when her husband united them all in a single noisy activity. She accepted at once. Margaret, with her mother’s permission, agreed just as readily. Marianne, though always reluctant to join any of their parties, was persuaded to go as well by her mother, who could not bear to see her shut herself away from any possible amusement.

The young ladies went, and Lady Middleton was happily rescued from the dreadful solitude that had threatened her. The gathering was exactly as dull as Elinor had expected. It produced not one new thought or expression, and nothing could have been less interesting than everything they said, both in the dining room and afterwards in the drawing room. The children followed them into the latter, and while they stayed there, Elinor was too certain of the impossibility of securing Lucy’s attention even to try. They left only when the tea things were taken away. The card table was then set out, and Elinor began to wonder how she could ever have hoped to find time for conversation at the park. Everyone rose to prepare for a round game.

“I am pleased,” Lady Middleton said to Lucy, “that you are not planning to finish poor little Annamaria’s basket tonight. I am sure working at paper filigree by candlelight must be bad for your eyes. We shall find some way tomorrow to make up to the darling little creature for her disappointment, and then I hope she will not mind it very much.”

The hint was sufficient. Lucy immediately remembered what was expected of her and answered, “Oh, you have quite misunderstood me, Lady Middleton. I am only waiting to find out whether you can make up your party without me; otherwise I should already have started my filigree. I would not disappoint the little angel for anything in the world. And if you need me at the card table now, I am determined to finish the basket after supper.”

“That is very good of you. I hope your eyes won’t suffer. Will you ring for some candles to work by? I know my poor little girl would be terribly disappointed if the basket were not finished tomorrow. Although I told her it certainly would not be ready, I am sure she is counting on having it done.”

Lucy immediately pulled her work table towards her and sat down again with a readiness and good humour which suggested that she could imagine no greater pleasure than making a paper-filigree basket for a spoiled child.

Lady Middleton suggested a rubber of Casino for the others. Nobody objected except Marianne, who, with her usual disregard for the ordinary forms of politeness, exclaimed, “Your Ladyship must kindly excuse _me_. You know how I hate cards. I shall go to the piano; I haven’t touched it since it was tuned.” Without any further ceremony, she turned from them and walked over to the instrument.
Lady Middleton’s expression suggested that she thanked heaven _she_ had never said anything so rude in her life.

“You know Marianne can never stay away from that instrument for very long, ma’am,” Elinor said, trying to soften the offence. “And I can hardly wonder at it myself: it has the finest tone of any piano I have ever heard.”
The five who remained were now ready to draw cards.

“Perhaps,” Elinor went on, “if I draw a card that leaves me out, I could help Miss Lucy Steele by rolling some of her papers. There is still so much to do on the basket that I really think she cannot possibly finish it tonight by working alone. I should enjoy it very much, if she would let me have a share in the work.”
“I should be extremely grateful for your help,” Lucy exclaimed. “I find there is more work left than I expected, and it would be dreadful to end by disappointing dear Annamaria after all.”
“Oh, it really would be dreadful!” said Miss Steele. “The dear little creature—how fond I am of her!”

“That is most kind of you,” Lady Middleton said to Elinor. “Since you really enjoy the work, perhaps you would be just as happy to wait until another rubber before joining us. Or would you rather take your chance now?”

Elinor gladly accepted the first suggestion. With a little of the tact Marianne could never lower herself to use, she had secured her own wish and pleased Lady Middleton at the same time. Lucy attentively made room for her at once. The two young rivals were thus seated next to each other at the same table, working in perfect harmony on the same task. Fortunately, Marianne’s piano was very close to them. Absorbed in her music and her own thoughts, she had by now forgotten that anyone else was in the room. Elinor therefore decided that, protected by its sound, she could safely introduce the subject that interested her, with no danger of being overheard by the people at the card table.
